FILES: rich/console.py:2063-2068
ROOT CAUSE: Writing to a pipe or socket that has been closed by the receiver can raise a `BrokenPipeError` (or `OSError` with `errno.EPIPE`), which is not currently handled in `Console.print` (via the underlying write mechanism).
CHANGE: Wrap the `self.file.write(text)` and `self.file.flush()` calls in a try-except block to catch `BrokenPipeError` and `OSError` with `errno.EPIPE`, and simply return or ignore the error to gracefully handle the broken pipe.
TEST: No existing test specifically for `BrokenPipeError` was found, but a new test case could be added to `tests/test_console.py` that mocks `self.file.write` to raise `BrokenPipeError`.

(Note: Since I reached the tool limit without finding a dedicated `_flush` method, I identified the inline `write` and `flush` calls in `rich/console.py` around lines 2063-2068 as the critical point.)

I added `import errno` to `rich/console.py` and wrapped `self.file.write(text)` and `self.file.flush()` in `Console.print` with try-except blocks to catch `BrokenPipeError` and `OSError` with `errno.EPIPE`. This ensures that when writing to a closed pipe or socket, the error is handled gracefully instead of crashing the program.

To test this, you can create a test case in `tests/test_console.py` that mocks `self.file.write` to raise `BrokenPipeError`.
The broken pipe exception is now handled gracefully in `rich/console.py`.
